reasoning_summary: 0001 OK: restates the problem with n=1012, sets of size n inside [2n], any 3 sets meeting in <=1 element. 0003 OK: announces a 4-set construction. 0005 OK: 2*floor(n/2)+2*ceil(n/2)=2n, so such a partition of [2n] into A,B,C,D exists. 0007 OK: each of A∪C, A∪D, B∪C, B∪D has floor(n/2)+ceil(n/2)=n elements, and the four sets are distinct. 0009 OK: any three of them, e.g. (A∪C)∩(A∪D)=A and A∩(B∪C)=∅; by symmetry every triple intersects in ∅, so <=1 element. 0011 OK: states the goal of the upper bound. 0013 OK: notation. 0015 OK: standard k x 2n incidence matrix, rows=sets, columns=elements. 0017 OK: legitimate double-counting object (triples of rows all carrying a 1 in a fixed column). 0019 OK: each of the k rows has exactly n ones, so the matrix sum is kn = sum of column sums c_i. 0021 OK: a column with c_i ones contributes exactly C(c_i,3) such triples; total = sum C(c_i,3). 0023 OK: Jensen over 2n columns with mean (kn)/(2n)=k/2 gives sum C(c_i,3) >= 2n*C(k/2,3), using the convexified function of step 0070 which agrees with C(c,3) at nonnegative integers. 0025 OK: sets up the reverse count. 0027 OK: three sets meet in <=1 element, so a fixed row triple is realized in at most one column, giving total <= C(k,3). 0029 OK: combining, 2n*k(k-2)(k-4)/48 <= k(k-1)(k-2)/6; dividing by k(k-2)/6>0 (valid for k>4) yields 2n <= 8(k-1)/(k-4). 0031 FAILS: at k=5 the RHS is 8*(5-1)/1 = 32 (not 8*5/1 = 40), and either way it is far LESS than 2*1012 = 2024; the asserted inequality '8*5/1 > 2*1012' is numerically false, and as written it points the wrong way — if the RHS really exceeded 2n there would be no contradiction at all, so step 0033 would not follow. The intended (and correct) reading is 2n = 2024 > 32 = RHS, contradicting 0029. 0033 OK only after repairing 0031 and adding the (true, unstated) fact that 8(k-1)/(k-4) strictly decreases for k>4, so the contradiction at k=5 propagates to every k>=5, forcing k<=4. 0035 OK given the repair: the argument actually gives k<=4 for all n>=17 (k <= 4(n-1)/(n-4) < 5 iff n>16), and with the construction of 0005-0009 the maximum is exactly 4; 'n>=21' is a weaker but true claim, covering n=1012 and answering the posed problem with 4. 0037 OK: label. 0039 OK: for 2n=6 the bound 6 <= 8(k-1)/(k-4) holds for every k>4 (RHS decreases to 8 > 6), so the triple count gives no bound; switching to counting (1,1) pairs is a valid alternative. 0041 OK: each row has n ones giving C(n,2) column pairs, so k*C(n,2) in total. 0043 OK: a pair of elements lying in 3 sets would give those 3 sets an intersection of size >=2, so each of the C(2n,2) column pairs supports at most 2 rows, total <= 2*C(2n,2). 0045 OK: k*n(n-1)/2 <= 2*2n(2n-1)/2 gives k <= 4(2n-1)/(n-1). 0047 OK: correct caveat that a counting bound need not be attained. 0049 OK: n=3 gives k <= (4*5)/2 = 10. 0051 OK as exposition (no mathematical claim). 0053 OK: label. 0055 FAILS (independent second error): equality in 0045 forces every pair of elements to lie in exactly 2 subsets, which forces every element to lie in 2(2n-1)/(n-1) = 5 subsets when n=3 (also directly kn/(2n) = 10*3/6 = 5), not 3; the author's own construction in 0059 has element 1 in five sets, and step 0065 uses 5.5 as the average, contradicting this line. 0057 OK: this is exactly the equality condition of the counting in 0043. 0059 OK: the 10 listed triples are distinct and every one of the 15 pairs from {1,...,6} occurs in exactly 2 of them (10*3 = 30 = 15*2 pair slots), so no 3 of the sets share 2 elements; the bound 10 is attained and the OP's guess of 8 was not optimal. 0061 OK: label. 0065 OK: 11 sets give 33 incidences over 6 elements, so some element z lies in at least ceil(33/6) = 6 sets. 0066 OK: those 6 sets contribute 12 non-z slots among the 5 remaining elements, so some y occurs at least ceil(12/5) = 3 times, and those 3 sets share {y,z}, a contradiction; hence k <= 10 for n=3. 0067 OK as a remark: the argument does start from the target value 11. 0069 OK: an open question, no claim. 0070 OK: the naive C(x,3) is indeed not convex on all of [0,2] (second derivative x-1 < 0 for x<1), so Jensen needs the modified function. 0072-0073 OK: the piecewise function is continuous at x=2 with left slope 0 and right slope 1/3 and is convex on x>2, hence convex on R, and it agrees with C(c,3) for nonnegative integers c, which is what steps 0021-0023 require. Overall: the mathematics of the main result (answer 4 for n=1012) is essentially sound, but step 0031 as written is false and reverses the inequality that produces the contradiction, and step 0055 states a false equality condition contradicted by the proof's own construction.
